newsitem.title: CHINA: Asia-Pacific central bankers hold China meeting.
newsitem.headline: Asia-Pacific central bankers hold China meeting.

text.p: Asian central bankers began a meeting in Shanghai on Friday amid market expectations of heightened cooperation after weeks of turmoil in regional currency markets.

Officials of the 11 participating regional central banks and monetary authorities declined to comment to reporters as they filed into the Shanghai hotel conference room where the one-day closed-door meeting was being held.
The group had scheduled a news briefing for 5.30 p.m. (0930 GMT) after they finished their discussions.

It was the second annual meeting of the governors of member countries of the conference, formally known as the Executives' Meeting of East Asia and Pacific Central Banks. The first was held in Tokyo last July.

Some analysts have hailed the meeting as the Asian regional equivalent of the G7 grouping and have built up hopes of some agreement on cooperation to stabilise currencies that have come under speculative attacks on foreign exchange markets.
In the morning session, each country would outline its own economic situation, said an official of China's central bank, the People's Bank of China.
In the afternoon, the governors would sum up their work over the last year while three working groups would discuss bank supervision and management, currency policy and financial markets, he said.
No detailed statement of the agenda was available, but the lingering turmoil in the foreign currency markets was expected to be high on the list of items to be discussed.

Thailand was the most vulnerable economy to the speculative onslaught and the nation was the first in the region to allow a de facto devaluation of its currency, the baht, with a managed float on July 2. Since then the baht has lost about 20 percent of its value.
The onshore Thai baht rate slumped to a new low of 32.70 on Thursday before recovering slightly while the Singapore dollar fell to a 33-month low of 1.4785.

The Philippines has also been forced to effectively devalue the peso and Indonesia has allowed the rupiah to float more freely. Malaysia is also believed to have used large amounts of its foreign exchange reserves to defend the ringgit.

Regional monetary authorities have come to each other's aid in the past. The monetary authority of Singapore intervened in the foreign exchange markets recently to help to shore up the sagging Thai baht.

In May, the central banks of China and Thailand signed a bilateral repurchasing agreement as part of regional cooperation to stabilise currencies in a time of emergency. Thailand has similar agrements with other neighbouring countries.
The People's Bank of China is host for the conference, chaired by its governor, Dai Xianglong.
The conference includes officials from Australia, China, Hong Kong, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, New Zealand, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand.
